name: Death
upright: Every ending planned: data kept as long as law and business require, then destroyed beyond recovery; access cut on the last day.
reversed: Records hoarded forever, wiped drives that still whisper, end-of-support servers left running, ex-staff who can still log in.
vision: An armored skeleton rides a white horse through the archive, ending everything on schedule. Its black banner bears a white rose with a date inked on every stem; the rider cuts no stem a day early or a day late. A bishop waves a magnet over a glass chip, and the chip only laughs. Disks the rider has already wiped still whisper names when held to the ear. At the gate the rider takes a departing knight's badge before the knight finishes saying goodbye. The sun rises between two towers: one has stopped selling bread, the other has barred its doors for good. On the river, a locked chest becomes driftwood the moment its only key sinks.
decode: The rider cuts each rose stem on its inked date → retention: keep data as long as law, regulation and business need require, then destroy it on schedule.
The chip that laughs at the magnet; wiped disks still whispering → degaussing cannot erase SSDs, and data remanence survives deletion: purge or destroy instead.
The badge taken before goodbye → deprovisioning: disable every account the moment employment ends; ex-staff accounts left active are a classic audit finding.
Two towers, one stops selling, one bars its doors → EOL: the vendor stops selling the product; EOS: patches and support end, so isolate or replace it.
The chest lost when its only key sinks → cryptographic erasure: destroy the encryption keys and the data is unreadable; ideal for SEDs and cloud storage.
facts: NIST SP 800-88: clear (overwrite; stops simple recovery), purge (degauss, block or crypto erase; stops lab recovery), destroy. Media leaving your control needs purge.
Privilege creep is access piling up as people change roles. On every transfer, remove old rights as new ones are added; access reviews catch what slips through.
Owners classify data and set its protection; custodians carry it out day to day (backups, restores); administrators grant access by the owner's rules.
trap: The collective once kept everything forever, just in case. Data held past its retention period is pure liability, discoverable in lawsuits and exposed in breaches; destroy it on schedule unless a legal hold applies.
